examples: 여권 있어요?
Do you have your passport?
Bare noun + 있어요? is the everyday way to ask; no particle needed in casual speech.
공항에서 여권을 보여줬어요.
I showed my passport at the airport.
여권을 보여주다 is the fixed collocation for presenting it; 을 marks the object.
여권을 잃어버려서 대사관에 갔어요.
I lost my passport so I went to the embassy.
Real-trip trouble: 잃어버리다 (lost-and-can't-recover) is stronger than plain 잃다.
nuance: 여권 is the official booklet that proves your identity and nationality when you cross a border. The hanja is 旅券 (旅 travel + 券 ticket/certificate), literally a 'travel certificate'. Do not confuse it with 비자 (visa), the separate permission to enter a particular country — you carry one 여권 but may need many 비자 inside it. The habitual partner verbs are 여권을 보여주다 (show), 여권을 발급받다 (get it issued), and the dreaded 여권을 잃어버리다 (lose). The English-speaker pitfall is the sound-alike 여건, which means 'conditions/circumstances' and has nothing to do with travel — keep the ㅝ in 여권 crisp, and remember it never takes a plural -s even when you mean several.

mistakes: Saying 여권을 만들다 ('make a passport') as if you craft it yourself. You don't make it; the government issues it, so the natural verb is 여권을 발급받다 (have it issued).

examples: 서울을 관광했어요.
I sightsaw around Seoul.
관광하다 can take the place directly as object — 서울을 관광하다.
주말에 시내 관광을 했어요.
I went city sightseeing on the weekend.
시내 관광 is the natural noun chunk; 을 marks it as the object of 하다.
이 도시는 관광으로 유명해요.
This city is famous for tourism.
관광으로 유명하다 is the set phrase for 'famous for tourism', with 으로 = 'by means of'.
nuance: 관광 means going around to enjoy famous places and scenery as a relaxed visitor. The hanja 觀光 literally means 'observe (觀) the light/glory (光)' — an old phrase for admiring a region's fine sights. Contrast it with 여행 (travel), the broader word for any journey: 여행 covers the whole trip including transit and rest, while 관광 zooms in on the act of touring attractions, so a beach vacation is 여행 but circling temples is 관광. Also distinguish 출장, a business trip — never call a work assignment 관광. It pairs as 관광을 하다, 관광 명소, 관광지. The pitfall for English speakers: 관광 is the activity, not the person; the tourist is 관광객 (next entry), so you cannot say '관광 came'.

examples: 여기 관광객이 많아요.
There are a lot of tourists here.
관광객이 많다 is the go-to phrase for a busy spot; 이 marks the subject.
외국인 관광객이 사진을 찍어요.
Foreign tourists are taking photos.
외국인 관광객 (foreign tourist) is more natural than 외국 관광객 in modern speech.
벚꽃 철이면 관광객이 몰려요.
When cherry-blossom season comes, tourists flock in.
관광객이 몰리다 paints a vivid 'crowds pour in' image.
nuance: 관광객 is a person visiting a place for sightseeing and fun, not a resident. The hanja 觀光客 adds 客 (guest) to 관광, so it literally reads 'sightseeing guest'. The nearest near-synonyms are 여행객 and 여행자: 관광객 stresses someone touring attractions, 여행객 is the neutral 'traveler' you'd see on signs and transport notices, and 여행자 leans literary/individual ('a traveler' in a story). For people from overseas, modern Korean prefers 외국인 관광객 (foreigner-tourist) over the older 외국 관광객. It collocates with 관광객이 많다, 관광객이 몰리다, 관광객으로 붐비다. English-speaker pitfall: don't drop the 객 and say 관광 for the person — 관광 is only the activity, so the human always needs the 객 suffix.

usage: buying it for the purpose of keepsake
examples: 기념품 샀어요?
Did you buy any souvenirs?
Casual question drops 을; 기념품 사다 is the core collocation.
친구한테 줄 기념품을 골랐어요.
I picked out a souvenir to give to my friend.
줄 (to give) + 기념품 shows the typical gift framing.
이 컵을 기념품으로 샀어요.
I bought this cup as a souvenir.
기념품으로 = 'as a souvenir'; 으로 marks the role the item plays.
nuance: 기념품 is a small item you buy on a trip to remember the place or hand out to people back home. The hanja 記念品 breaks down as 記 (record) + 念 (think of/remember) + 品 (article) — an 'article for remembering'. Compare 선물 (gift) and 특산품 (local specialty): every 기념품 you bring home can become a 선물, but 선물 is any present given for any reason, while 특산품 names the region's signature product (잠실 호두과자, 제주 감귤). The habitual partners are 기념품을 사다, 기념품 가게, 기념품으로 사다. English-speaker pitfall: don't call every trip purchase a 선물 — if its purpose is to commemorate the trip it's a 기념품, and note that the buying verb is 사다, not 'get', so '기념품을 사다' rather than a literal '얻다'.

Using 얻다 ('obtain/receive for free') for buying souvenirs. You pay for them, so the verb is 사다 — '기념품을 샀어요', not '기념품을 얻었어요'.

usage: to have a lot of luggage
examples: 짐 다 쌌어요?
Have you finished packing?
짐을 싸다 'pack'; casual speech drops 을 and adds 다 (all).
호텔에 짐을 맡기고 나왔어요.
I left my luggage at the hotel and went out.
짐을 맡기다 = entrust/check bags; 에 marks where they stay.
이사할 때 짐이 정말 많았어요.
When I moved, I had a ton of stuff.
짐 also covers a household's belongings, not just travel bags.
nuance: 짐 is a pure-Korean word (no hanja) for the bags and belongings you carry when you travel or move — often heavy. Its opposite-pair verbs are key: 짐을 싸다 means 'pack' and 짐을 풀다 means 'unpack', a fixed antonym set worth memorizing together. Compare 수하물, the formal airline/airport term you see on signs ('checked baggage'), versus everyday 짐 you'd say out loud. Note 짐 stretches beyond suitcases to all your household goods during a move, and figuratively to a 'burden' (마음의 짐, a weight on the heart). English-speaker pitfall: 짐 is uncountable like English 'luggage', so never pluralize it; and to 'pack' you say 짐을 싸다 (literally 'wrap the load'), not a literal translation of 'put in'.

examples: 캐리어 무거워요.
The suitcase is heavy.
Adjective 무겁다 + bare noun; everyday spoken style.
공항에서 캐리어를 부쳤어요.
I checked my suitcase at the airport.
캐리어를 부치다 is the fixed verb for checking baggage in.
기내용 캐리어 하나만 가지고 탔어요.
I boarded with just one carry-on suitcase.
기내용 (for-cabin-use) + 캐리어 names a carry-on precisely.
nuance: 캐리어 is the hard, wheeled suitcase with a pull-up handle that you roll behind you. It is a loanword from English 'carrier', but beware: this is a Konglish narrowing — to an English ear 'carrier' suggests a phone carrier or aircraft carrier, while Korean 캐리어 means specifically the rolling suitcase (English calls it a 'suitcase' or 'roller bag'). Contrast it with 가방, the umbrella word for any bag, and with 여행 가방 (travel bag), which can be soft-sided. Because it has wheels, the signature verb is 캐리어를 끌다 (pull/wheel it), not 들다 (lift) — and for flying you 캐리어를 부치다 (check it). English-speaker pitfall: don't say 캐리어를 들다 unless you're literally lifting it off the ground; rolling it is always 끌다.

usage: carry a heavy one on the back
examples: 배낭 메고 가요.
I'm going with my backpack on.
배낭을 메다 'wear on the back'; -고 links to the next action.
배낭에 물이랑 김밥을 넣었어요.
I put water and gimbap in the backpack.
에 marks where you put things; 이랑 = casual 'and'.
대학생 때 유럽으로 배낭여행을 갔어요.
In my college days I went backpacking in Europe.
배낭여행 (one word) is the set term for budget backpacking trips.
nuance: 배낭 is the large bag you carry on your back for hiking or rough-and-ready budget travel. The hanja 背囊 is 背 (back) + 囊 (pouch/sack), literally a 'back-sack' — fitting, since the defining verb is 배낭을 메다, 'sling it on your back'. Compare 가방 (any bag, including a handbag or briefcase) and 책가방 (a school bag): 배낭 specifically sits on both shoulders and implies the outdoors or 배낭여행 (backpacking). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: English 'carry/hold a backpack' tempts learners into 배낭을 들다 (hold in the hand), but anything worn on the back takes 메다 — so 배낭을 메다 for wearing it, 들다 only if you're carrying it by the strap in your hand. Pack-it verbs are 꾸리다 and 싸다.

examples: 숙소 어디예요?
Where's your accommodation?
Bare noun + 어디예요? — the natural way to ask where someone's staying.
인터넷으로 숙소를 예약했어요.
I booked the lodging online.
숙소를 예약하다 = reserve a stay; 으로 marks the means (online).
밤늦게 숙소에 도착해서 바로 잤어요.
I reached my lodging late at night and fell straight asleep.
에 marks the destination; 숙소에 도착하다 = arrive at one's lodging.
nuance: 숙소 is the general word for any place you stay overnight on a trip — hotel, guesthouse, motel, or a friend's spare room. The hanja 宿所 is 宿 (lodge/spend the night) + 所 (place), literally 'a lodging place', which is exactly its scope: it names the function, not the building type. Contrast it with the specific 호텔 (hotel) and with 집 (home), where you actually live — never call your travel stay 집. The natural collocations are 숙소를 잡다 (informally 'snag a place'), 숙소를 예약하다 (reserve), and 숙소에 묵다 (lodge there). English-speaker pitfall: 숙소 is a place, so you go 숙소에 (to it) with the 에 particle, and you 묵다 or 머물다 there — don't borrow the English 'stay' as a noun and try to make 숙소 do a verb's job.

Using 살다 ('live/reside') for a short stay. For lodging a few nights you 묵다 or 머물다 — '숙소에 묵어요'. 살다 implies long-term residence, which sounds wrong for a hotel.

examples: 오늘 일정 어때요?
What's today's schedule like?
Bare 일정 + 어때요? asks casually about the day's plan.
여행 일정을 미리 짰어요.
I planned out the travel itinerary in advance.
일정을 짜다 = work out a schedule; 짜다 means 'weave/assemble' a plan.
회의 때문에 내일 일정이 다 바뀌었어요.
Because of a meeting, tomorrow's whole schedule changed.
일정이 바뀌다 (intransitive) = the plan changes on its own; 이 marks subject.
nuance: 일정 is the planned schedule of where you go and what you do, day by day — for a trip, but equally for work or events. The hanja 日程 is 日 (day) + 程 (journey/measure), an 'apportioning of the days'. Distinguish it from 시간 (time, clock time) and 계획 (plan): 시간 is just the hour on the clock, 계획 is the broad intention ('I plan to save money'), while 일정 is the concrete time-tabled sequence of items. Note the signature verb 짜다 — you 일정을 짜다 (literally 'weave a schedule'), the same verb used for 계획을 짜다. Watch the adjective 빡빡하다 / 바쁘다 for a packed itinerary. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 시간 when you mean the agenda — '오늘 시간이 어때요?' asks if someone is free, but '오늘 일정이 어때요?' asks about the day's plan.

examples: 이제 출발해요.
We're leaving now.
출발하다 turns the noun into 'depart'; this is how you announce setting off.
기차 출발 시간을 확인했어요.
I checked the train's departure time.
출발 시간 is the fixed compound for 'departure time'.
눈 때문에 비행기 출발이 두 시간 늦어졌어요.
Because of snow, the plane's departure was delayed two hours.
출발이 늦어지다 = the departure gets pushed back; 이 marks subject.
nuance: 출발 means leaving to begin a journey — the moment a person or vehicle starts moving away. The hanja 出發 is 出 (go out) + 發 (set off/issue), 'going out and setting forth'. examples: 방금 도착했어요.

도착 시간을 친구한테 알려줬어요.

도착 시간 is the set compound; 한테 marks the person you inform.
밤늦게 호텔에 무사히 도착했어요.

도착하다 takes the place with 에 — 호텔에 도착하다 — plus 무사히 'safely'.
